H&P – Detailed

Consult Summary:
45-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus on methotrexate presents with same-day onset of shortness of breath, right-sided pleuritic back pain, low-grade subjective fever and two episodes of haemoptysis; clinically stable on video assessment. Face-to-face review for suspected chest infection arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Shortness of breath and sharp pain in right posterior chest/back when taking a deep breath.  
• Onset/Progression: Began earlier today; pain and dyspnoea constant since onset.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Coughed up small amounts of blood-streaked sputum twice today.  
  – Subjective “slight fever” (temperature not measured).  
  – Awareness of heartbeat (“can feel my heart beating”), no documented palpitations during consult.  
  – Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance and increased effort with daily activities for ~2 weeks.  
• Exacerbating factors: Deep inspiration increases pain.  
• Relieving factors: Not stated.  
• Pertinent negatives: No recent long-haul flights; no leg pain/swelling; no known prior clots; non-smoker.

Past Medical History:
• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); current disease activity not discussed.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• Methotrexate – dose/route/frequency not documented (last taken this morning).  
Allergies: Denies medication or other allergies.

Social History:
• Occupation: Office desk job.  
• Living situation: Lives alone in a flat; owns a cat.  
• Tobacco: Non-smoker.  
• Alcohol/recreational drugs: Not discussed.

Family History:
• Denies family history of venous thrombo-embolism; no other family history recorded.

Physical Examination:
Vitals: Pulse 66–74 bpm, regular (patient-counted). Temperature, BP, RR, SpO₂ not recorded.  
General: Appears clinically stable on video.  
Skin/Perfusion: Capillary refill normal.  
HEENT: Oropharynx normal on video; no cervical lymphadenopathy on self-palpation.  
Cardiovascular/Respiratory/Abdominal/Neuro: Not examined via video.  
Musculoskeletal: Not examined.

Investigations:
• None performed yet.  
• Planned: In-clinic assessment today for auscultation, vital signs, possible CXR and labs.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Acute pleuritic chest pain with haemoptysis in an immunosuppressed patient most likely due to community-acquired pneumonia/chest infection; however pulmonary embolism and methotrexate- or SLE-related pulmonary pathology must be considered.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Community-acquired pneumonia – supports: fever, pleuritic pain, cough with haemoptysis, immunosuppression; opposes: no auscultatory findings yet.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – supports: classic triad (+ SLE risk); opposes: normal pulse, no provoking factors.  
3. Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis / alveolar haemorrhage – supports: on methotrexate; opposes: very acute onset and presence of fever.

Issue 1 – Possible pneumonia / chest infection  
• Arrange same-day face-to-face GP review for full examination (lung auscultation), vitals (BP, HR, RR, SpO₂, temperature).  
• Consider chest X-ray if examination suggests pneumonia or if no improvement.  
• Empiric oral antibiotic likely after evaluation (no known drug allergies).  
• Safety-net: seek urgent care if worsening breathlessness, high fever, increased haemoptysis, chest pain, or collapse.

Issue 2 – Rule out pulmonary embolism  
• During face-to-face visit: perform clinical probability assessment (e.g., Wells score), check oxygen saturation; consider D-dimer or immediate referral for imaging (CTPA) if indicated.  
• Counsel patient on signs of PE (sudden worsening SOB, pleuritic pain, syncope).

Issue 3 – Methotrexate / SLE-related pulmonary complications  
• Review methotrexate dosing and recent monitoring; hold medication if concern for drug-induced pneumonitis after clinical review.  
• Assess SLE activity and consider rheumatology input if lupus pneumonitis or alveolar haemorrhage suspected.

General plan items  
• Reassure regarding low immediate suspicion of lung cancer; advise follow-up imaging if symptoms fail to resolve.  
• Provide practice support number; ensure patient booked for in-person assessment today.  
• Document encounter and communication.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Objective vitals (BP, RR, SpO₂, temperature) and lung auscultation pending face-to-face visit; medication dose/frequency not documented; alcohol history not discussed.  
● No direct conflicts between transcript and DDx noted, but patient gave two different names (“Tracy” then “Doris”) – administrative discrepancy.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; minor conversational overlaps.
